20 New Hot Wheels and Matchbox Collectibles for 2026 and 2027
68 photos
Photo: Lamley Group
I’ve successfully managed to convince my family and friends to stop buying clothes for me on special days. They’ve turned to diecast collectibles instead, and I just got a Hot Wheels 3-pack and two Silver Series models today.
I guess deciding on these can still be stressful for them though, as they’re aware how hard it can be to get the ones I don’t already own. But hey, I appreciate the gesture, and I’ll use some of them for one of my future unboxing stories (the ones that are new to me as well). Right now, I’m trying to figure out if I’m ready to buy a few more Red Line Club models, or if I should postpone it all for 2027.
Mattel’s line-up for next year certainly looks impressive, but you know how it goes: the nicer the car, the lower the chances to get it for the regular retail price. Seeing as Mr. Lambert shot this video during the 40th Annual Hot Wheels Collectors Convention in Los Angeles last month, the Datsun 240Z is already sold out on Mattel Creations. And I imagine the upcoming Dodge Challenger SRT won’t last long either.
With those two out of the day, let’s focus on the next few releases instead! The Volkswagen T1 Rockster is this year’s special, Holiday collectible. It’s almost certain it won’t be as rare as the 2023, Spectraflame Purple variation I have at home. Back then, the production limit was set at 30,000 units, while the company only made 4,000 units of the Rockster for is debut.
The 1969 Ferrari 312 P is also coming up this year, and it has lost both the Redline wheels and the special paint job in the process. I guess the team in El Segundo would have upgraded it to a Chase if the licensing agreement would have allowed for a Chrome model. The second variation of the 1995 BMW M3 LTW is no longer just a simple RLC collectible, as it will be next year’s official membership car.
The 2027 Membership Car is a BMW Photo: Lamley Group It gets a new finish, new wheels and it obviously comes with the Membership Patch many people enjoy collecting. Brendon Vetuskey’s RLC-Exclusive Custom '72 Datsun 240Z is getting close to its 10th anniversary, but this new purple version is only the seventh iteration so far. It used those exact same 4-spoke Real Riders wheels in 2019, and only 10,000 units of that car ever left the factory.
It’s no wonder some people seem to think it’s worth $400. Am I the only one who instantly thinks of Japan Historics when seeing those rims? Is that theme dead in the water at this point, or do you still think it can still move forward? Anyway, it would be amazing if someone pulled some strings to use all-Spectraflame paintjobs for the five (or six) cars inside, especially seeing how exciting the next 1998 Subaru Impreza WRX STI is.
Gold really isn’t my thing, and it often annoys me when the manufacturer uses this approach to “highlight” a certain model. I realize some of you may have enjoyed the Spectraflame Slate/Red color combo we had this year, but next year’s iteration is so much more of a showpiece: I wouldn’t be surprised to bump into something like it at the SEMA Show .
I’ve said this before and I’ll say it again: the 1994 Porsche 911 Turbo 3.6 S 'Package' has what it takes to become of the most desirable Hot Wheels items in 2027 across the board. These days I’m happier to go after one of Zuffenhausen’ classics than drool over something that came out from Italy. It’s especially valid after having driven and experienced five different 911 Turbo generations in the past three years alone.
A Viper is coming to the Red Line Club Photo: Lamley Group You could dedicate an entire year to collecting Hot Wheels Dodge Vipers , and it might not be enough to find them all. I’ve collected many of these tiny replicas before, so I almost feel compelled to go after the 1997 GTS Coupe. The car in the video is an EP sample, so don’t get all worked up about the colors or small problems (no headlights or taillights).
I’d say there’s still a good chance the First Edition will use a blue finish with white stripes, which doesn’t mean I’d take yellow or red out of the equation just yet. And of course you can get a look at the V10 engine inside, as it would have been downright ridiculous if the team in El Segundo opted for opening doors instead of an opening engine cowl. With Dwayne Vance’s Ford GT40 MKII, the plan seems to be recreating the iconic 1-2-3 finish from the 1966 24 Hours of Le Mans race.
Bruce McLaren and Chris Amon’s #2 car showed up last year, while Ken Miles and Denny Hulme will get their turn in 2027. I hope we won’t have to wait until 2029 for the #5 version! As much as I like the Honda Civic Type R, the new RLC casting feels underwhelming to me for some reason: could it have something to do with it having a Chase version? It’s just so much safer going out of “hype’s” way if you know what I mean.
I often find so much more joy in the obscure models that sometimes even end up as peg-warmers just because they don’t have Liberty Walk/Pandem/RWB in the name. I have nothing against those brands, but the fatigue is real at this point. The BMW 2002 Jun Imai designed in 2012 is starting to show its age, and the Collector Edition release wasn’t that effective in bringing it back into the spotlight.
Basic and Premium models are a bonus Photo: Lamley Group Dwayne Vance’s approach is about to turn up the heat to 11 with some rally-derived elements and an apparent improvement in the way the engine bay looks like. I’m by no means a BMW fan and I still want a closer look at this thing. Once you finish looking at the RLC -focused photos, you’ll stumble upon a closer look at one very special Team Transport set for next year.
Drifty Seven is a new concept that’s coming for the Mainline HW Future Past series: I don’t recall ever seeing a 1957 Chevy all geared up for drifting, although the United States has had a few old school muscle cars going down that path. While Mr. Vetuskey mentioned the 1969 AMC SC/Rambler is one of his bucket list castings, something that he always wanted to do, I can’t share that same level of enthusiasm unfortunately.
All we know for now is that it’s headed for the 2027 Car Culture series, which once again makes me think Mattel might just revive the Dragstrip Demons theme at last. Brendon’s 1989 Ford Mustang LX won’t roll on Real Riders wheels, but it will be part of the Drag Racers mini-collection alongside Larry Wood’s Draguar (the new casting with an opening body).
Seeing this Mustang reminds me of our trip to Kiskunlachaza for the European Drag Racing event a few years ago: who doesn’t love a 10-second (or faster) car? As for the ZZ Top CadZZilla, don’t worry about the wheels: that’s just an intermediate stage in creating a new casting! Now, let’s see what’s up with the Matchbox Off-Road set! Right off the bat, it looks like deja-vu to me.
Matchbox is reviving one of Ryu Asada’s old castings Photo: Instagram/User ada_3l3 I kept thinking I must have already reported on the five cars inside, although the card art certainly didn’t remind me of anything.
I’ve developed a bit of a soft spot for the Volkswagen Beetle 4x4, as I’ve unboxed two or three variations in the past few years already. It’s the oldest casting on the list, and one of the two that Ryu Asada himself designed.
I’m referring to the Baja Bullet here, which has been around since 2010, but hasn’t had a new release since 2022. It might sadly be the set’s unofficial peg-warmer, and the MBX Field Car could suffer the same fate.
At least that’s what I think will happen in my community, as I know what other fellow collectors are typically into. The 1948 Willys Jeepster and the '70 Datsun 510 should be quite effective, though, and I might even pick one of them up for a photo shoot if the opportunity arises.

This Papago Camper Van Pairs a Calm, Welcoming Interior With Serious Off-Road Credentials
16 photos
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Papago Vans
Today's featured build is based on a 2026 AWD Mercedes-Benz Sprinter with a 170" wheelbase. It was created by Papago Vans, a Mesa, Arizona-based company specializing in personalized camper van conversions designed for adventuring.
As always, let's start the tour with the exterior. For starters, the Sprinter rides on Black Rhino wheels wrapped in Nitto Ridge Grappler all-terrain tires. This is a good wheel and tire combo to make the most out of the vehicle's AWD capabilities.
Papago Vans took things even further and improved the off-road capabilities by fitting a Van Compass Stage 4.3 suspension kit, which comes with front and rear adjustable shocks and a rear mini leaf spring pack.
At the front, you'll come across an FVC (Flatline Van Co.) bumper complete with a bullbar, two light pods, two amber fog lights, two recovery shackles, and a Warn Evo 12S winch rated for 12,000 lb. (5,447 kg).
On the opposite end, the company installed a spare tire carrier/ladder combo, as well as another carrier that holds a storage box with an extra dry compartment on top of it.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Papago Vans An FVC Apex ladder on the driver's side offers quick and easy access to the roof, where you'll discover an FVC Safari rack. It holds two 200 W solar panels, light pods on the sides, a front-facing Morimoto BigBanger light bar, a flat-mounted Starlink antenna, and a Nomadic Cooling awning with an integrated light strip.
Other notable exterior mods are power and water hookups, FVC rocker lockers, and AMP Research powered steps that come out when you slide the main door. There's also a set of flares on the sides.
Flares, also known as pods or capsules, are designed to increase the van width. This, in turn, allows you to fit a bed inside in an east to west arrangement instead of the standard north to south. This rig's Vanspeed capsules are finished in matte black and come with half-slider windows.
Enter, and a warm and tastefully designed interior will greet you. The customer opted for off-white cabinetry, a slatted ceiling with recessed LED strips, and wood-imitating vinyl plank flooring. The look is complemented by a white subway tile kitchen backsplash and mint green cushion upholstery.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Papago Vans The interior has an open layout, with no wall separating the driver's cabin from the living space. The driver and passenger seats are mounted on swivel bases, meaning they can be turned around to face the back of the van.
Straight ahead of the entrance, Papago Vans devised a seating area. It has a single-person bench with an integrated Lagun mount. Above, you'll find a large cabinet that hides the "command center" for the utilities.
It includes a touchscreen display that lets you monitor and control the power and water systems, as well as switches for the water heater, water pump, shower drain, and freeze protection system.
Next, we have the kitchen on the passenger side. It features a dual-burner induction stovetop, a microwave oven, a deep stainless steel sink with a cutting board cover, and a flip-up table that provides additional counter space.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Papago Vans A Maxxair vent fan positioned above the kitchen will help draw out the smells and fumes from cooking. Moreover, for storage, you can use an overhead cabinet, three drawers, and two lower cabinets.
A floor-to-ceiling unit on the opposite side integrates an overhead cabinet and a tall fridge with a freezer compartment. Beside it, you'll come across a simple but practical bathroom.
The bathroom boasts a shower with a handheld wand, a portable Laveo dry-flush toilet, a ceiling light, and a black Nautilus self-cleaning retractable door. Moreover, the walls are finished with real white tiles.
Most of the time spent in this van when not driving will be in its back part. There, Papago Vans devised a transformable lounging and sleeping area.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Papago Vans The lounge setup consists of a U-shaped couch made up of two connected benches and a large table in the middle. Turning it into a sleeping arrangement is simple: drop the table to the same height as the benches, add extra panels, and rearrange the cushions.
However, that isn't the main sleeping arrangement. Above the lounge area, the builders installed a Lippert elevator bed, with its bottom part finished to match the van's ceiling.
At the push of a button, you can lower the bed to your preferred position and hop in to go to sleep – no need to set up the bed or arrange anything. The elevator bed offers a full-size memory foam mattress.
The two benches in the lounge area accommodate the utility systems. Power is on the left – the electrical system's highlights are a 920 Ah battery bank and a 3,000 W Victron inverter/charger. You can use three charging sources to keep the batteries topped off: solar power , shore power, and DC-DC charging while the engine is running.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Papago Vans On plumbing, the van is equipped with a 4-gallon (15-liter) Bosch electric water heater, a freshwater tank inside the van, and an under-mounted greywater tank.
There are two more important systems in this van that make it suitable for four-season adventuring: a 12V rooftop A/C unit and an Espar heater tapped directly into the vehicle's fuel tank.
Open the van's two rear doors, and you'll gain access to a storage compartment integrated into the rear bench. Next to its door, Papago Vans added a battery monitor, a shut-off switch for the power system, and two light switches.
All in all, this Papago Vans camper is fully loaded and ready to help its owner create unforgettable memories of off-road and off-grid adventures, all while traveling in comfort and style.

Original Owner Couldn't Sell 700k-Mile 1964 Mustang for $30K, Did the Only Reasonable Thing Left
15 photos
Photo: Grant Martin
Here’s something we don’t see everyday. Or ever, to be fair. Two years ago, I came across an ad for a 1964 Mustang. The car was offered for sale – and that detail alone was enough to catch my attention. Then I learned just how special this particular car was: a one-owner example with some seven hundred THOUSAND (700,000) miles on the clock. And the price was almost too good to be true. The car now sits in a museum, where it belongs better than in any other private garage.
Back in 2024, this extraordinary 1964 Ford Mustang hardtop coupe surfaced on the classic car market, carrying a story that bordered on mechanical mythology. Bought brand-new in late May 1964 and kept by the same dedicated custodian, Mr. Grant Martin, for nearly 62 years, the pony car boasted 700,000 miles (1,126,541 kilometers) on its odometer. With an initial asking price of $25,900, it looked like the undisputed classic car steal of the millennium.
To put that astronomical distance into perspective, this early-production pony car had covered the literal equivalent of a round trip to the Moon, plus another one-way journey to Earth's natural satellite. Presented for sale as a gleaming, restored coupe still running its original 260-cubic-inch (4.3-liter) V8 engine, the 2024 listing offered six decades of unbroken single-owner provenance for less than the price of an entry-level modern compact crossover.
Yet the collector car market can be a strangely fickle arena, and the expected stampede of appreciative buyers never materialized. Mr. Martin kept his beloved 1964 Mustang up for sale for about 1 year, eventually trimming the asking price from $25,900 down to $24,900 in hopes of finding the right caretaker. Instead of attracting purists who valued its history, the listing became a magnet for bargain hunters and relentless lowballers.
Photo: Facebook/Kansas City Automotive Museum Throughout that entire year-long ordeal, only one prospective buyer stepped forward with an offer that actually met the asking price , a gentleman who was almost 70 years old and had never owned a Mustang before. Every other offer fell painfully short of the mark. One particularly brazen individual offered $20,000, declaring that figure was top price and adding that he would wait by the phone for the call to sell. He’s probably still day-dreaming.
That condescending pitch sealed the fate of the attempted sale. The seller informed the $20,000 bidder on the spot that he would donate his Mustang before ever selling it for that amount. To several other lowballers, he replied that if they could find another car exactly like his for what they were offering, he would love to see a picture of it. Nobody ever replied, and Grant Martin withdrew the listing.
After pulling his car off the market, the owner hired a professional appraiser, who evaluated the 1964 Mustang at $36,000, proving just how generous the original $25,900 asking price had been.
Photo: Facebook/Kansas City Automotive Museum Looking closely at current market dynamics, the owner observed that many enthusiasts who bought and kept original 1964 to 1966 Mustangs have reached an age where they no longer need them and wish to sell. Even so, when he checked ClassicCars.com, he found 10 times the number of 1965 and 1966 Mustangs for sale compared to true 1964 models, confirming that earliest-production cars like his are rarely found these days.
Economic pressures have also reshaped the collector landscape, as the skyrocketing cost of living leaves fewer people with disposable income to spend on vintage hardware. Beyond the purchase price, the owner pointed out that keeping a classic vehicle requires dedicated garage space, spare time, mechanical know-how, specialized tools, and replacement parts. Rather than dealing with tire-kickers, he kept his word after nearly 62 years of ownership and donated the Mustang.
The beneficiary of that extraordinary generosity was the local Kansas City Automotive Museum, whose curators were delighted to welcome the high-mileage 1964 coupe into their collection and openly glad that online buyers had passed up the opportunity to purchase it. For the longtime owner, placing the pony car in a respected museum meant that even though he misses having it in his garage, he can visit it whenever he wants.
Photo: Facebook/Kansas City Automotive Museum To understand how a single automobile earned that level of lifelong devotion, the story goes back to April 1964, when the future owner, then in his early twenties, attended the New York World's Fair before returning for a second visit in May 1964. Inside the Ford Pavilion, young Grant saw the newly introduced Mustangs on display for the very first time and immediately decided that no other Detroit machine on the market could compare to it.
When asked why he gambled on an all-new model that nobody knew anything about instead of choosing an established nameplate, his answer was simple: the Mustang was the best-looking car he had seen to date that was still affordable. His stepfather strongly urged him to forget about the Mustang and buy a conventional Ford Fairlane instead, which is probably what he would have purchased had he not stood his ground.
Blue Oval loyalty was already well established in his household long before that spring day, as his family had owned several Fords in the years leading up to 1964, and the local Ford dealer was a personal friend of his stepfather. In late May 1964, the young man and his stepfather walked into that local dealership, where only one Mustang remained in stock on the showroom floor: a V8 coupe.
Photo: Grant Martin Grant had arrived at the dealership hoping to find a Mustang powered by the 289-cubic-inch (4.7-liter) V8, yet the lone hardtop left in inventory carried the smaller 260-cubic-inch (4.3-liter) V8 rated at 164 horsepower and 258 pound-feet (350 Newton-meters) of torque. That 260-cubic-inch (4.3-liter) mill proved more than adequate over the decades. Buying his very first car required a loan that took two-and-a-half years to pay off, at $76 monthly.
From the moment he drove off the lot, the new Mustang saw heavy action on American highways, logging almost 30,000 miles (48,280 kilometers) during its very first year on the road. Although his first wife drove the coupe once in a while, he was essentially the sole driver throughout more than 61 years of ownership, building an intimate mechanical bond with the vehicle that few motorists ever experience in life.
While the Mustang was his very first car and permanent companion, he and his first wife did sample two other memorable imports over the years. They bought a 1965 Mercedes-Benz 230SL hardtop with 19,000 miles (30,578 kilometers) on the odometer for $3,700, and after selling the German sports car, they purchased a 1972 Datsun 240Z for about $4,000, fondly recalling that both stick-shift machines were wonderfully fun cars to drive.
Photo: classiccars.com None of those other rides could eclipse the memories forged inside the 1964 Mustang. His fondest memory of all was touring the American West and climbing into the Canadian Rocky Mountains near Banff, Alberta, before driving south through Glacier National Park and Yellowstone National Park on his way back home to Illinois. That epic cross-country loop proved that an early pony car could conquer mountain passes as effortlessly as boulevards.
Not every highway excursion was quite so leisurely. One of the craziest stunts he ever pulled behind the wheel came the day he decided to see how fast he could cross the 300 miles (483 kilometers) of Iowa from west to east. He blitzed the entire stretch in 3.5 hours, averaging nearly 86 mph (138 kph), earning a speeding ticket, and vowing never to repeat it.
Another crazy behind-the-wheel adventure unfolded on New Year's Eve in 1978, when he departed Omaha, Nebraska, at 8 p.m. for a 7.5-hour winter drive to St. Cloud, Minnesota. As the outside temperature plunged to -20 degrees Fahrenheit (-29 degrees Celsius), the Mustang's heater core failed after the first hour on the road. He pushed onward until about 11 p.m. before finally stopping at a roadside motel, frozen to the bone.
Photo: classiccars.com By the next morning, conditions had worsened to -25 degrees Fahrenheit (-32 degrees Celsius) with a biting 15 mph (24 kph) north wind and about 5 hours of driving still ahead. Inside the unheated cabin, his feet froze so badly that he could barely walk, forcing him to pull over roughly every 50 miles (80 kilometers) in search of an open gas station just to thaw out and warm up.
Throughout that brutal ordeal, his thoughts turned to the freezing bomber crews of World War II flying for hours at high altitudes over Germany in -20 degrees Fahrenheit (-29 degrees Celsius) cold, where many suffered frostbites. His own father was among those many brave young airmen, though tragically his plane was shot down and the entire crew was lost.
He promptly had the heater core replaced so that it never happened again. Because the Mustang was his first car, he never once considered selling it during those earlier decades. That attachment became painfully clear when the coupe was stolen, leaving him depressed for quite a while until authorities returned the car after two months. Funny enough , the police had recovered it two hours after the owner reported it missing.
Photo: classiccars.com What he always loved most was the timeless 1964 styling, which still looks great today compared to modern vehicles that have “virtually no styling and all look alike”. I couldn’t agree more, Mr. Martin.
Still, logging 700,000 miles (1,126,541 kilometers) exposed every flaw in Ford's early engineering. He disliked the wide turning radius, the moisture traps designed to eventually rust out, and the cheap cardboard used for the glove box and heater ducts instead of metal or plastic. He is deeming it very unprofessional – and six decades of continuous ownership (well, minus the months the Mustang was in police custody) grant him the right to say that out loud.
Another factory shortcoming nearly cost the owner his life. The original automatic choke proved dangerously unreliable and almost got him killed at a railroad crossing, prompting him to replace it with a dependable manual choke. In retrospect, Mr. Grant Martin notes that serious engineering design only began with the 1967 Mustangs. Even so, he drove the coupe regularly until 2004, when his second wife insisted that he retire the Mustang for a modern car.
Photo: classiccars.com Taking the Mustang off daily duty in 2004 launched a comprehensive two-year restoration project that cost more than $40,000 by itself. When asked to estimate his lifetime operating expenses across fuel, insurance, servicing, numerous sets of tires, and three transmission rebuilds, he admitted he cannot calculate the figure and would likely shudder if he knew the exact total. Remarkably, his original 260-cubic-inch (4.3-liter) V8 engine has needed only one overhaul.
Many enthusiasts have wondered how that original 260 V8 managed to last so long across six decades of driving. The owner attributes its longevity to strict preventative maintenance , specifically changing the engine oil and filter every three months regardless of mileage. Just as importantly, he never used ethanol-blended gasoline in the Mustang, pointing out that ethanol can easily ruin older classic car engines and delicate internal fuel system components.
Photo: startribune.com Octane ratings also played a major role in preserving the vintage V8. Back in the 1960s, regular gasoline was 92 octane while premium gasoline reached 95 octane, whereas modern gas stations typically offer 87-octane regular or 91-octane premium fuel. The owner once tried running 87-octane regular gasoline, but it immediately caused his engine to knock, so he stayed exclusively with the 91-octane fuel for which the powerplant was originally designed.
It shouldn’t make any difference now, with his trusty companion now settling for a new role, as a museum exhibit – one of the greatest ever in the history of the little Ford pony car. Truth be told, there isn’t a quantifiable amount of valuables in the world that could possibly buy that history, the countless memories, and the ownership experience that Mr. Martin has enjoyed with his 1964 Ford Mustang along the 700,000 miles of life-long adventures. You did the car justice, Sir. Thank you!

EICMA 2026 • 2027 Suzuki SV-7S Unveiled at the EICMA Show in Italy: I’m Suddenly More Nostalgic Than Ever
1992 Mercedes-Benz 500 E, the Merc With Porsche Flavor, Sold In Less Than a Week Since Its Listing
9 photos
Photo: Garage Kept Motors / Instagram
It sat proudly in the inventory of Grand Rapids, Michigan-based Garage Kept Motors , though it did so for less than a week since it was showcased on social media – the first time we checked it out, it was already gone from the list of available rides. No worries, we still tracked it down because it’s absolutely cool to look at, and it was a shame not to give it five minutes of fame.
The Mercedes-Benz W124 is a range of executive cars made by Daimler-Benz from 1984 to 1997, and it was absolutely instrumental to the premium German automaker’s modern development because in 1993 the series officially transitioned to the iconic E-Class moniker.
It was also conceived in a multitude of body styles: the W124 was actually only the sedan, and there were also the estate (S 124); coupé (C 124); cabriolet (A 124); limousine (V 124); rolling chassis (F 124); and even a long-wheelbase rolling chassis (VF 124). It was also the model that AMG used to conceive the legendary AMG Hammer 6.0 and introduced the E36 AMG models for the estate, coupé, and cabriolet when the series was facelifted and changed to the E-Class.
Before that, just a couple of years earlier, in 1991, Mercedes had a wacky proposition for its fans: the 500 E (renamed to E 500 after 1993), a high-performance version of the W124 created with ample help from none other than Porsche, partially assembled by the latter and only with painting done at the Mercedes Sindelfingen plants while final assembly was again done in Zuffenhausen.
Well, if you wanted to own a piece of Mercedes’ quirky history with Porsche , sadly, the occasion has passed. By the time we got around to discussing this 1992 Mercedes-Benz 500 E that we saw on social media courtesy of Grand Rapids, Michigan-based Garage Kept Motors, it was gone in less than a week after it got its beauty photo shoot plastered on Instagram.
True, the YouTube feature was uploaded one week earlier, but the showroom photos are always pretty boring and don’t do justice to many of these vehicles. Alas, this Merc is way too beautiful not to deserve its five minutes of fame, which actually turned into at least half an hour of drooling and oozing at the gallery of photos.
So, this 1992 Mercedes-Benz 500 E was offered with just 102,400 miles on the odometer, meaning that it didn’t sit hidden in a vault all of its life and instead went out and enjoyed it to the max out there on the wide-open roads. That’s pretty cool in itself, and the silver-over-gray setup is pretty traditional for a Mercedes of the era, powered by the naturally aspirated 5.0-liter V8 engine derived from the 500 SL (R129) roadster, with the braking components also coming from the same direction.
“The 500E is definitely an ‘if you know, you know’ sleeper with nothing more than some minimally flared fenders with some larger wheels and brakes filling the spaces. Nothing else advertises the fat 322 horsepower hiding under the hood,” says the description, and sometimes that’s all it takes to put a grin on the driver’s face: knowing that the hillbilly next to them can be left in a cloud of dust with a surprised look on his ignorant face. Cool, right? Right!

I’ve spent countless hours here at Electrek doing detailed hands-on testing of hundreds of electric bikes. Through thousands of miles of riding, I’ve been fortunate to learn these e-bikes inside and out, top to bottom and front to back. That long-term experience with real-world e-bike testing has helped me find the best electric bicycles on the market for just about any budget.
Below are some of the top e-bikes I’ve hand-tested for every price range, current as of November 2026. These are probably the best deals you’ll find all year on electric bikes, meaning this is the best time ever to get a new model! Check out the awesome e-bikes below, any one of which could become your next electric bike.
This list is divided into several price ranges. We’ll start with the best e-bikes under $1,000, then move on to the under-$2,000 category, under-$3,000 category, etc. The goal is to highlight some of my favorite models in various budget ranges to help you make the right decision based on your needs and budget.
Best electric bikes under $1,000
The sub-$1,000 electric bike category is critical for a few reasons.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
First, it’s pretty hard to produce a quality e-bike and sell it for under $1k. Most of the options in this price category make too many sacrifices in quality or longevity to earn a spot on this list as one of “the best.”
Second, many newly curious e-bike buyers just aren’t prepared to drop several thousand dollars on a brand-new concept, making this price range critical for many new e-bike shoppers.
Fortunately, we’ve found some excellent options for cheap electric bikes that can still save you some serious dough.
Lectric XP LITE 3.0
The Lectric XP LITE 3.0 was recently updated and is now quite likely the king of bang-for-your-buck electric bikes.
For a while now, the $999 Lectric XP 4 has reigned supreme in the budget electric bike category. That’s still a great bike, and we’ll discuss it next, but the more affordable $799 Lectric XP LITE3 is an even more wallet-friendly electric bike.
That new e-bike offers some great riding at under 800 bucks.
It’s a throttle-enabled Class 2 folding electric bike with 20″ wheels, a max speed of 20 mph (32 km/h), and a motor rated for 300W continuous and 819W peak. It’s not going to be the strongest hill climber in this list, but it does get going quickly on flat and modestly hilly terrain.
And the biggest features include quality hydraulic disc brakes, color LCD screen, turn signals, and even an optional Gates carbon belt drive system for an extra $100. Riders can also opt for a nearly double-sized battery for an extra $200.
This is the only e-bike in this price range that I know of with a 48V electrical system. All the other budget e-bikes under $800 use a 36V system and thus suffer from weaker power.
There are some things that you give up with this model, such as that the fenders aren’t included free. But for just $799 , you’re still getting built-in lights, a hidden battery, large color LCD display and a lightweight folder. Plus it comes in lots of fun color options.
There’s a lot of value there!
Lectric XP LITE3 quick specs
Motor: 300W (819W peak) geared rear hub motor
Top speed: 32 km/h (20 mph)
Range: Claimed up to 72 km (45 mi) or 130 km (80 mi) with long-range battery
Battery: 48V 7.8 Ah (375 Wh) on the base model
Weight : 22 kg (49 lb)
Price : $799
Lectric XP4
The Lectric XP4 is the undisputed best-selling electric bike in the US. The bike has racked up massive sales figures as riders flock to its extreme bang-for-your-buck. Simply put, it’s hard to find any other e-bike that offers this level of value!
The XP4 can get riders up to 28 mph (45 km/h) and now comes in either a 500W or 750W version, with respective battery sizes of 48V 10.4Ah and 48V 17.5Ah. The long-range version’s premium price tag ( $1,299 vs the standard range model at $999 ) is perhaps even higher value than the already impressive base model.
Other upgrades include a new stronger rack design, torque sensor for smoother pedal assist, and improved hardware like the 8-speed transmission, hydraulic disc brakes, updated urban/trail hybrid-style tire tread, and a beautiful new TFT color screen.
The XP4 is hands-down the highest value e-bike I’ve ever tested and it’s quite obvious just how much time and effort went into building such a potent e-bike designed to fit so many different riders and tasks.
It’s hard to find a better combination of low cost and high performance anywhere in the e-bike market right now.
Lectric XP4 quick specs
Motor: 500W or 750W geared rear hub motor (peaks at ~1,000W and ~1,300W)
Top speed: 45 km/h (28 mph)
Range: 45-85 miles (70-135 km) depending on battery choice
Battery: 48V 10.4Ah (500 Wh), or larger 17.5Ah (840Wh) battery choices available
Weight : 69-71 lb (31-32 kg)
Price : $999
Ride1Up Portola 02
When Ride1Up launched the original Portola , it was pretty obvious what the game plan was: fire a shot across Lectric Ebike’s bow with a direct competitor to the Lectric XP line. By all accounts, Ride1Up nailed it with an impressive competitor. Now the company has come back with the next generation of the bike , this time attempting to take on both the XP line and XP Lite from Lectric. That’s thanks to two models, the Portola 02 , and the stripped-down Portola 02 Lite .
The Ride1Up Portola 02 has a lot more going for it than just the attractive starting price of $895 for the Lite or $995 for the full-size bike with frame-integrated rack. The models offer great performance with a maximum speed of 28 mph (45 km/h) and good quality components including hydraulic disc brakes, torque sensor, front suspension, a built-in rear rack (except for the Lite), and a 750W motor.
There are two battery options available, either a 48V 10Ah or a 48V 15Ah, and the larger battery only costs an extra $100, so it’s quite worth the extra 50% range.
I love the sleek-looking frame and apparently, I’m not alone. Those who are on the hunt for a good-looking folding fat tire e-bike that doesn’t break the bank will likely find this to be one of the more fashionable options.
Ride1Up Portola 02 Lite
Ride1Up Portola 02 quick specs
Motor: 750W geared rear hub motor
Top speed: 45 km/h (28 mph)
Range: Claimed up to 72 km (45 mi), but less if you’re heavy on the throttle
Battery: 48V 10 Ah (480 Wh), or larger 48V 15 Ah (720 Wh) battery available
Weight : 26-28.5 kg (58-63 lb depending on options)
Price : starting at $895
Best electric bikes under $2,000
Once you bump up above the $1,000 limit, you start to see many more great options for e-bikes in a wide range of categories.
From electric cargo bikes to cruisers and even electric mopeds, there’s something for everyone in this price range.
JackRabbit OG2 micro e-bike
The $1,249 JackRabbit OG2 is in one of these fuzzy areas between e-bikes and other e-rideables. In this case, it straddles the line between an electric bike and an electric scooter.
It more or less feels like an electric bike based on its ride geometry. However, the lack of pedals means that it could also be classified as an electric scooter, albeit a large-wheeled e-scooter.
But with those 20-inch wheels and bicycle seat, the JackRabbit OG2 rides much more like a small folding e-bike than an e-scooter. And its electronics match that of a light e-bike, too.
The 300W motor gets the little runabout up to 20 mph (32 km/h). The small 158 Wh battery only offers around 10 miles (approximately 16 km) of range, but is also conveniently small enough to easily keep a spare battery in a cargo pocket or even a small purse.
The biggest benefit of the JackRabbit is that it is so simple that the lack of frills keeps the weight down to just 25 lb (11.3 kg)! For an e-bike, that’s almost so light that it floats.
The company also released a higher power and larger battery capacity version too , which might be good for riders who want to push harder and go farther. For those that want to see a few more upgrades on this minimalist e-bike, the JackRabbit OG2 and XG might be more your size.
See my full review of the JackRabbit OG2 here .
JackRabbit OG2 quick specs
Motor: 300W geared rear hub motor
Top speed: 32 km/h (20 mph)
Range: 20 km (12 mi)
Bike weight: 11.3 kg (25 lb)
Brakes: Rear mechanical disc brake
Price : $1,249
Lectric XPedition 2.0
We called the Lectric XPedition e-cargo bike a runaway success right from the start, and that’s exactly what it turned into. Now with the new Lectric XPedition 2.0 on the road, it’s better than ever.
With heavy-hauling weight capacity, the option for one or two batteries for extra long range, hydraulic disc brakes and torque sensor-based intuitive feeling pedal assist, this e-bike is dragging electric cargo bikes into the future.
The $1,399 Lectric XPedition 2.0 has turned the electric cargo bike market upside down, bringing a heavy-hitting cargo e-bike to market for an ultra-affordable price.
While it’s not the fanciest cargo e-bike on the market (you’ll find those in the $4,000-$6,000 price range further down this article), it’s definitely the best bang for your buck thanks to a combination of high value parts and reasonable pricing.
Lectric XPedition 2.0 quick specs:
Motor: 750W rear hub motor
Battery: 48V 14Ah (672 Wh) with the option for a second battery (and higher capacity batteries)
Top speed: 28 mph (45 km/h)
Range: up to 75 miles (120 km)
Weight: 74 lb (33.5 kg)
Price: $1,399
Heybike Ranger 3 Pro
The Heybike Ranger 3 Pro is probably one of the best deals in full-suspension folding e-bikes right now. With a combination of a powerful motor, comfortable geometry, front & rear suspension, and a high-tech interface that includes NFC card unlocking, the Heybike Ranger 3 Pro is punching above its weight class.
In fact, that’s its main drawback, its weight. It’s a heavy bike, but the speed and power mean heavier motors and batteries, so you know you’re going to be carrying a more robust powertrain around with you.
But between the performance and the looks, this is one awesome comfortable ride that just doesn’t break the bank! I had a blast reviewing it , and I’ll bet you’ll have a blast riding it!
Heybike Ranger 3.0 Pro quick specs
Motor: 750W rear hub motor
Top speed: 28 mph (pedal assist), 20 mph (throttle)
Battery: 48V 15Ah (Samsung cells)
Range: 55 miles (claimed), ~40 miles real-world
Suspension: Front hydraulic fork + rear shock
Price: $1,499
Aventon Soltera.2
The $1,399 Aventon Soltera.2 is the latest version of Aventon’s beautiful city bike that offers some of the best quality fabrication that I’ve seen in this price range – or even in higher price ranges. It is offered in either a single-speed or seven-speed format.
The bike rolls on narrow tires for that efficient city ride, while still packing in a 500W motor.
The battery is a bit smaller at 36V and 10Ah, but the bike makes up for a smaller battery by being able to integrate it into the frame in a sleek and attractive package.
The beautiful color display also adds to the bike’s charm, as do the powerful headlight and frame-integrated tail light. There’s even an awesome companion app that lets your phone track your bike’s important stats. Basically, you’re getting a lot for $1,199 here!
Check out my in-depth Aventon Soltera.2 review here .
Aventon Soltera.2 quick specs:
Motor: 500W peak-rated rear hub motor
Battery: 36V 10Ah (360 Wh)
Top speed: 20 mph (32 km/h)
Range: 20-63 miles (32-101 km)
Weight: 46 lb (21 kg)
Price: $1,199
Aventon Soltera
Ride1Up Roadster V3
Ride1Up has proven itself as a high-value electric bike brand, focusing largely on efficient and speedy commuter e-bikes. While the company has many models in the $1,000 to $2,000 range, the $1,295 Ride1Up Roadster V3 is one of the best bang-for-your-buck options in the lightweight category.
This 500W-rated e-bike offers Class 3 performance, meaning you can hit speeds of up to 28 mph (45 km/h), or a still impressive 20 mph (32 km/h) if using the throttle. But sticking to pedal-assist means you get to enjoy that quality torque sensor for smoother pedaling. The bike even comes with an option for either a belt drive or a 10-speed Shimano transmission, and three frame sizes to choose from.
The V3’s design was updated with many new features, including a now-removable battery for even more convenient charging both on and off the bike. And with a sub-40 lb weight, it’s hard to beat this one on a pound-for-pound basis!
Ride1Up Roadster V3 quick specs:
Motor: 500W rear hub motor
Top speed: 45 km/h (28 mph)
Range: 32-64 km (20-40 mi) throttle vs. pedal assist
Battery: 36V 10Ah (360 Wh) with genuine LG cells and UL certified
Weight : 17.6 kg (39 lb)
Price : $1,295
Check out my full review of the Ride1Up Roadster V3 here :
Lectric XPeak2
Lectric Ebikes expanded into larger territory with the launch of the Lectric XPeak2. It was the company’s first e-bike with a larger than 20″ wheel size, bringing some chunky 26×4.0″ tires into the company’s inventory.
The XPeak takes the form of a typical adventure-style fat tire electric bike. It features a hardtail design with a suspension fork, high-volume tires, hydraulic disc brakes, and a relatively large battery that is certified by the Swiss testing agency SGS to meet UL 2849 standards.
The bike is also tested to higher standards for ruggedness of the frame and fork than most e-bikes in this price range, meaning it’s likely going to last longer too. As far as fat tire adventure-style e-bikes go, there’s no better bang for your buck than the Lectric XPeak2.
Lectric XPeak2 quick specs:
Motor: 750W (1,300W peak)
Top speed: 45 km/h (28 mph)
Range: Up to 75 km (45 mi) on low power
Battery: 48V 15 Ah (720 Wh)
Weight : 39.4 kg (67 lb)
Price : $1,499
Lectric XPeak2
Ride1Up Prodigy V2 Eco mid-drive e-bike
The $2,295 Ride1Up Prodigy V2 Eco has brought new meaning to the phrase “low-cost mid-drive electric bike”, updating an already impressive e-bike with a new next-gen setup.
This e-bike sports a high-end German-manufactured Brose mid-drive motor and can hit speeds of up to 28 mph (45 km/h), yet is price similarly to much cheaper hub motor-based electric bikes.
It’s a perfect commuter e-bike for someone who wants high-quality parts like that German mid-drive motor with 90Nm of torque, hydraulic disc brakes, bright LED lights, included fenders, rear rack, and a very comfortable saddle. Plus, there’s a choice between a step-over or a mid-step frame to better fit a wider variety of riders.
This e-bike is easily worth another $700 more than the price tag, if not more. In fact, you’ll find many of these same components on e-bikes with $2,000-$3,000 price tags all over the place. So if you’re looking for a higher quality e-bike that doesn’t cost as much as a fancy bike shop e-bike, this is the one to consider.
Ride1Up Prodigy V2 Eco quick specs:
Motor: Brose TF Sprinter mid-drive
Top speed: 28 mph (45 km/h)
Range: 30-50 miles (50-80 km)
Battery: 36V 14Ah (504Wh)
Weight : 58 lb (26 kg)
Price : $1,295
Ride1Up Vorsa
The Ride1Up Vorsa is Ride1Up’s most versatile “SUV‑style” e‑bike yet, designed to transition seamlessly from commuting through city streets to loaded errands and light gravel or park paths. With a standard price around US $1,495 , it delivers an exceptionally high‑value riding experience that often outperforms models far above its price range.
With a powerful 750 W rear‑hub motor producing a hefty 95 Nm of torque (and peaking over 1,400 W in real-world tests), the Vorsa accelerates comfortably and can maintain Class 3 speeds of up to 28 mph via pedal assist or 20 mph throttle thanks to its dual-sensor system and customizable display. Whether you’re hauling cargo or cruising commute lanes, the Vorsa delivers smooth, responsive power that feels natural and planted.
I love how well‑rounded the package is. Ride1Up outfits the Vorsa with a 100 mm suspension fork, comfortable ergonomic bars, multiple colors/frame styles (step‑thru or standard), and a modular rear rack rated for 440 lb total payload, which is expandable via Connect+ accessories. Hydraulic disc brakes, full fenders, integrated lighting, and passive features like UL‑certified batteries and Apple FindMy integration round out the build.
At just $1,695 , the Ride1Up Vorsa is priced way below fair market value, which makes this an absolute steal of a deal.
Check out my Ride1Up Vorsa review here , and also check out the new expansion to the Vorsa line with lighter and heavier duty models built on the Vorsa platform.
Ride1Up Vorsa quick specs:
Motor: 750W rear geared hub motor
Top speed: 45 km/h (28 mph)
Range: 50-100 km (30-60 mi)
Battery: 48V 15Ah (720 Wh)
Weight : 29 kg (65 lb)
Price : $1,495
Ride1Up Vorsa
Monarc Marker electric adventure bike
The Marker is the first model unveiled by the e-bike brand spun out of Lectric eBikes, known as Monarc. The brand leverages Lectric’s size and buying power to bring higher end bikes than we typically see in the budget space – complete with higher shelf components – but at better prices and with better customer service.
The Monarc Marker is a powerful, Class 3-capable fat tire adventure e-bike with powerful four-piston brakes, a quality reverse arch suspension fork, Shimano CUES transmission, and comes with two batteries, all for an incredible reasonable MSRP of US $1,999.
Monarc also made waves by offering a 5-year warranty as well as 12-hour customer service five days a week, ensuring customers feel comfortable knowing they are buying from a company that will stick around to support riders long after the purchase is complete.
Learn more about the Monarc Marker here , or check out its current sale price here .
Motor : 750W (1,638W peak) rear-geared Bafang hub motor
Top speed : 28 mph (45 km/h)
Battery : 2x 48V 15Ah (720 Wh) for a total of 1,440 Wh
Range : Up to 40 miles (65 km) per battery, or 80 miles (130 km) with two batteries
Price : $1,999
Juiced Scrambler
When Juiced returned with a vengeance after being saved by Lectric, the brand did so with two impressive new Scrambler models: a hard tail and a full-suspension bike. They’re both awesome moped-style e-bikes and handle great, but the full-suspension version definitely kicks things up a notch and allows for even wilder riding.
But since they share the same features and performance outside the rear suspension, either would make an awesome addition to your e-bike fleet. Basically, it’s a powerful yet street-legal e-bike that is designed for real-world riding, thanks in no small part to its designer, Austin Homes, being a seasoned competitive bike racer across multiple disciplines and bringing that keen eye to the Scrambler’s development.
Juiced Scrambler quick specs:
Motor: 750W continuous-rated rear hub motor
Top speed: 28 mph (45 km/h)
Range: Up to 60 miles (up to 98 km)
Battery: 52V 19Ah (988 Wh)
Weight : 83-85 lb (37.6-38.5 kg) for HT/FS, respectively
Price : $1,699 (HT) or $1,899 (FS)
Best electric bikes from $2,000 to $3,500
By the time you surpass the $2,000 mark, you’re starting to get into serious e-bikes with serious performance or build quality.
If you’re spending this much, you’ll want to ensure you’re buying from a reputable company with top-notch products and service.
Ride1Up TrailRush
The Ride1Up TraiRush is the first actually quite good electric mountain bike that comes in at a budget price. It gives you a real German-made Brose motor, which offers good power matched with whisper-quiet performance. You get a dropper seat post and Maxxis Minion tires, Tektro Orion quad-piston hydraulic disc brakes, and a 120mm Rockshox Judy Silver TK Air Fork.
The first time I took a ride on the Ride1Up TrailRush, I couldn’t believe just how good the bike felt, especially from a company known for its wide array of commuter and street-oriented electric bikes. But Ride1Up was founded by cyclists at heart, and so they know what it means to build a good bike, regardless of category. At $2,095 , this is a steal for just great parts.
Ride1Up TrailRush quick specs:
Motor: Brose TF Sprinter mid-drive
Top speed: 28 mph (45 km/h)
Range: 30-50 miles (50-80 km)
Battery: 36V 14Ah (504Wh)
Weight : 57 lb (25 kg)
Price : $2,095
Priority Current Plus
I love the $3,299 Priority Current electric bike so much that it has become one of my daily riders. It’s the one I grab when I’m doing city riding and I know I want to be pedaling.
While the original version was already a great bike, the new Current Plus adds some key improvements, such as an included throttle and a nearly 50% larger capacity battery for more range. The throttle is great in a pinch, but the bike is also just so much fun to pedal thanks to a torque sensor-based pedal assist that provides natural-feeling assistance up to a fast 28 mph top speed.
The internally geared rear hub combined with a Gates belt drive system and powerful hydraulic disc brakes make this a very nice e-bike for the price. Plus that mid-drive motor offers tons of torque (140 Nm!) for climbing hills or accelerating quickly.
I’m also a fan of the built-in lights and included fenders, not to mention the punchy hydraulic disc brakes and Goodyear tires.
Mid-drive electric bikes aren’t cheap, but the price is definitely a fair one for this e-bike.
Priority Current Plus quick specs :
Motor: 500W mid-drive motor with torque sensor
Top speed: 28 mph (45 km/h) or 20 mph (32 km/h) user-selectable
Range: 40-75 miles (64-120 km)
Battery: 720 Wh frame-integrated battery
Weight : 24 kg (53 lb)
Price: $3,299
Ride1Up CF Racer1
I’m not normally a carbon fiber, drop bar, race bike kind of guy. But then again, that’s usually because those types of bikes are way out of my price range… until now.
The Ride1Up CF Racer1 brings carbon fiber road e-bikes to the common man, offering both a traditional road bike and a gravel bike edition.
At under 29 lb (13 kg), these e-bikes are some of the lightest around. I picked one up with my index finger and was shocked at how easily it left the ground.
To get there, that meant a relatively low-power motor and a smaller battery were required. But for the folks that ride these types of bikes, a big motor and heavy battery probably aren’t on their wishlist anyway. Instead, a simple extra boost, as if you’ve always got a tailwind, helps augment your own pedaling.
For just $2,295 , there’s no better deal out there for a budget-friendly carbon fiber road e-bike.
Ride1Up CF Racer1 quick specs
Motor: 250W 42 Nm torque
Top speed: 28 mph (45 km/h) on pedal assist
Range: 16-40 miles (26-64 km)
Battery: 252 Wh frame-integrated battery
Weight : 12.9 kg (28.6 lb)
Price: $2,295
Ride1Up REVV1 FS
This full-suspension electric moped-style e-bike is a masterclass in high performance electric bike design. Sure, it’s an obvious SUPER73 imitation, but it’s a really well done imitation.
It handles well, it’s got great rubber between you and the road, the suspension gives a comfortable ride, and it’s got plenty of extra power.
Despite the 750W label, the e-bike can be unlocked to make use of nearly 1,500W of peak power. I was able to reach a top speed of 37 mph (59.5 km/h) during my testing (not on public streets!).
But the bike ships in Class 2 mode with a 750W limit and 20 mph (32 km/h) maximum speed, meaning you’ll have to contact the company to request an unlock for the bike to be used above Class 2 speeds and power levels.
All in all, the $2,395 Ride1Up REVV1 FS is an amazing e-bike for anyone who wants a moped-style ride with full-suspension, high quality 4-piston hydraulic disc brakes and a design that rides almost like a motorcycle, yet in a bike form factor.
Check out my complete Ride1Up REVV1 FS review here .
Ride1Up REVV1 quick specs:
Motor: Bafang 750W continuous rear hub motor
Top speed: 20 mph (32 km/h) out of the box, 37 mph (59.5 km/h) when unlocked
Range: 30-60 miles (48-96 km)
Battery: 52V 20Ah (1,040 Wh)
Weight: 93 lb (42 kg)
Price: $2,395
Tern Quick Haul
The Tern Quick Haul is an electric cargo bike from the famed cargo e-bike company Tern. It holds the distinction of being the most affordable model in Tern’s lineup.
That says a lot, because Tern is known for its high-quality e-bikes that are built to be ridden every day for real-world errands, carpool duty, and more. These e-bikes are meant to replace cars, and they do just that for many riders. With a huge list of accessories, you can outfit a Quick Haul for just about any job.
The Tern Quick Haul features a mid-drive Bosch motor, hydraulic disc brakes, Tern’s vertical parking rack, and a relatively lightweight but high utility design that is meant to carry just about anything in your life.
We had the chance to test a pair of Quick Hauls at Eurobike in Frankfurt last year, which you can learn more about here.
Motor: Bosch Active Line Plus mid-drive motor Top speed: 20 mph (32 km/h) with pedal assist (no throttle) Range: Up to 60 miles (96 km), less when riding in highest power Battery: 400Wh, removable/lockable Weight: 50 lb (22.8 kg) Price : $2,999
Ariel Rider X-Class
When it comes to fast, powerful electric mopeds on a budget, it’s hard to compete with the $2,399 Ariel Rider X-Class . This is the e-bike I usually recommend when someone simply wants the most power and speed for the least amount of money.
The impressive performance comes from a powerful 1,000W motor that actually puts out closer to 2,000W of peak power. It can be limited to 20 mph if you’d like, but I got it up to 36 mph in unlimited mode.
The bike rolls on 20″ moto-style wheels and comes with nice parts including hydraulic disc brakes, a bench seat, dual suspension, and a big moto-style headlight.
You can see my full review of the Ariel Rider 52V X-Class here .
Motor: 1,000W (2,000W peak) rear hub motor
Top speed: 36 mph (58 km/h), but can be limited to Class 2 speeds
Range: Up to 75 miles (120 km), less when riding at top speed
Battery: 52V 18Ah (936 Wh), removable/lockable
Weight: 80 lb (36 kg)
Price : $2,399
Ariel Rider X-Class
Xtracycle Hopper electric cargo bike
The Xtracycle Hopper is something of a Goldilocks cargo bike, in my opinion. It’s not as big as a traditional long tail cargo bike, but it’s still big enough to carry multiple kids or a week’s worth of groceries.
It’s also not as pricey as the expensive $5-7k bike shop cargo e-bikes, yet it’s much higher quality than the typical direct-to-consumer cargo e-bikes.
I’ve tested it for all sorts of cargo jobs and even put my friends and family on it to take their kids to school and let me know how it works for them. Everyone has come away impressed with the ride feel, which seems much more like a traditional bike than a bulky cargo bike.
For the money, the Xtracycle Hopper offers incredible value and much higher quality construction than you’d get with entry-level brands.
Check out my full Xtracycle Hopper review here .
Xtracycle Hopper quick specs:
Motor: 750W geared rear hub motor
Top speed: 45 km/h (28 mph)
Range: 32-80 km (20-50 mi) depending on throttle or pedal assist
Battery: 48V 15Ah (720 Wh)
Weight: 38.5 kg (85 lb)
Price: $2,499
Xtracycle Hopper electric cargo bike
Best electric bikes from $3,500 to $5,000
Above $3.5k, you’re entering some seriously dedicated e-bike territory.
These e-bikes either feature top-shelf components like drivetrain and brake parts, or pack in so much power that they couldn’t possibly be priced any lower.
Either way, you’re not in Kansas anymore. You’re heading down the e-bike rabbit hole.
Tern HSD
Tern is renowned for building high-quality electric bikes that double down on utility features. The newly updated Tern HSD is the company’s more affordable utility e-bike, offering many features you’ll find on its higher-end GSD but at a price that more riders can stomach.
The HSD uses small 20″ wheels and includes a folding stem, making it nice and compact. But taking it one step further, Tern outfitted it with its innovative rack that lets you park the bike on its tail, meaning it takes up barely more space than a coat rack in the corner of a room.
The bike’s Bosch mid-drive and high capacity batteries provide a high-end e-bike drive, and they are matched with a variety of performance drivetrain options that you can select from, depending on how high you want to spec the bike.
Whether you’re ferrying around kids or buying a week’s worth of groceries, the HSD is a solid option.
Check out my detailed first ride experience on the Tern HSD here .
Tern HSD quick specs:
Motor: Bosch Active Line Plus mid-drive
Top speed: 32 km/h (20 mph) with electric assist
Range: 42-110 km (26-69 mi) depending on pedal input
Battery: Bosch PowerPack 400 Wh
Weight : 25.4 kg (55.9 lb)
Price: $4,299
Xtracycle Swoop ASM
The Xtracycle Swoop ASM is one of those electric cargo bikes that makes you rethink the entire category.
Not only does it include high-quality components and fancy features like automatic shifting paired with a high-end Shimano mid-drive motor, but it also just feels like you’re riding a normal-sized bike instead of a long and awkward cargo e-bike.
I found I can even ride it without my hands on the bars because it tracks so straight and rides so stable. That’s a feat you can’t pull off with most budget cargo e-bikes since they aren’t designed with proper bicycle geometry. But Xtracycle is a true cyclist’s cargo e-bike company, and so they understand proper bicycle design.
Check out my full review of this incredibly high-end and comfortable-to-ride cargo e-bike here .
Xtracycle Swoop ASM quick specs:
Motor: Shimano STEPS EP6 Cargo
Top speed: 45 km/h (28 mph)
Battery: 630 Wh Shimano battery
Frame: 6061 aluminum
Suspension: Suntour MOBIE34 CGO-Boost 80mm travel coil with pre-load adjustment
Brakes: Tektro hydraulic disc brakes with 180 mm rotors
Weight : 31 kg (68 lb) without battery or accessories
Price: $4,999 or save $200 with discount code ELECTREK
Ariel Rider Grizzly
When it comes to all-wheel-drive electric bikes, the $3,299 Ariel Rider Grizzly is one of my favorites.
This incredible e-bike is really more of a small electric motorcycle. It uses two high-power motors – one in each wheel – to offer speeds in the mid-30s and acceleration that will get you there in the blink of an eye.
Full suspension and hydraulic disc brakes make this an e-bike that handles well at any speed, and the bright red paint job looks as aggressive as the e-bike feels. It even comes with footpegs pre-installed so you can carry a passenger with you.
Plus it’s got double batteries to feed those two power-hungry motors, so you’ll be able to ride this e-bike pretty darn far too, as long as you aren’t too demanding from the throttle.
Check out my full in-depth review of the epic Ariel Rider Grizzly e-bike here .
Ariel Rider Grizzly quick specs:
Motors: Dual 1,000W continuous hub motors (1,850W peak or 3.7 kW combined)
Top speed: 36 mph (58 km/h) when unlocked, but can be limited to Class 2 speeds
Range: Up to 75 miles (120 km), less when riding at top speed
Battery: 52V 35Ah (1,820 Wh) between two removable/lockable batteries
Weight: 105 lb (47.6 kg)
Price: $3,299
Priority Skyline
The Priority Skyline builds upon Priority Bicycles’ legacy of creating high-performance, low-maintenance e-bikes and ups the ante with more premium parts than we’ve ever seen on a Priority e-bike before.
The show stopper here is the inclusion of Pinion’s 12-speed automatic gearbox, which smartly shifts gears without the rider ever having to think about it. You can personalize your shift points to dial in the ride, and let the centrally-mounted gearbox do the rest. The carbon belt drive transfers your pedal power while a 750W rear hub motor brings the extra power riders need.
There are also high-quality hydraulic brakes, a great suspension fork, and a big battery for long range in the city. Rear rack and complete fenders come standard, as do the built-in LED lights and adjustable handle-bar stem.
See my full review of the Priority Bicycles Skyline here .
Priority Bicycles Skyline quick specs:
Motor: 750W hub motor with torque sensor
Top speed: 45 km/h (28 mph)
Range: Up to 96 km (60 mi) on pedal assist, less on throttle
Battery: Downtube-integrated and removable 720 Wh battery
Weight : 30.8 kg (68 lb)
Price: $3,999
Best electric bikes above $5,000
You just couldn’t stop, could you? I showed you plenty of awesome e-bikes that didn’t cost most of a paycheck. But you just haaaaaaad to keep going.
Fine, here they are. These are some of the most expensive e-bikes out there that we’ve tested and that I’d actually recommend someone buying, if you can pony up the cash.
GoCycle G4i+
When it comes to ultra-premium folding electric bikes, there’s only one name that comes to my mind: GoCycle. These are the most impressive folding e-bikes I’ve ever seen. And they better be – they were designed by a former McLaren engineer.
Between the carbon fiber work, single-sided wheels, high-tech tires, trippy LED dot display, innovative rear suspension, and completely enclosed drivetrain, there’s a lot of high-end stuff going on here.
The speed will vary from 15-20 mph depending on which country you buy the bike in, but the performance is only part of the equation. The quick folding and light, compact design of the e-bike is the real winner here.
Check out my full review of the GoCycle G4i+ here .
GoCycle G4i+ quick specs:
Motor: 500W front hub motor
Top speed: 20 mph (32 km/h) in the US
Range: up to 50 miles (80 km)
Battery: 36V 10.4Ah (375 Wh)
Weight : 37.2 lb (16.9 kg)
Price: $6,999
FREY EX Pro electric mountain bike
The FREY EX Pro is a high-end electric mountain bike with crazy high power. It uses the same motor as the CSC FT1000MD we featured above (the Bafang M620 mid-drive), but cranks up the current to provide closer to 1,500W of power.
It’s enough to destroy chains if you aren’t careful. We know. Several of us here at Electrek have done it.
The FREY EX Pro not only features high-end parts like a RockShox Lyric fork and Magura MT5e hydraulic brakes, but it even comes with dual batteries so you can ride farther and stay on the trails longer.
I’ve personally taken this e-bike back UP a downhill mountain bike course – that’s how powerful it is.
It may be expensive, but it saves you several thousand dollars compared to many European electric mountain bikes with similar components but a fraction of the power in the FREY.
See my full review of the FREY EX Pro here .

Top speed (tested): 59 km/h (36 mph)
Battery: Dual 48V 14Ah packs (1,344 Wh total)
Range: Varies considerably by ride style/terrain, but 30-100 km (20-60 miles) is the ballpark
Weight: 34 kg (75 lb)
Price: $5,580
Tern GSD
The Tern GSD improves upon the Tern HSD with even more capability and even nicer components. There are multiple versions that can take you up to nearly $10k, but even the lower-tier versions are not “low tier,” if you know what I mean.
Parts like automatically engaging electric locks, 10-speed Shimano Deore transmissions, Magura MT5e quad-piston hydraulic disc brakes, and more set these e-bikes apart from the rest of the pack.
If you’re getting a Tern GSD, you’re getting a fully qualified car replacement. There are many people who use these instead of buying a second car. When you look at it like that, the price suddenly seems pretty reasonable.
Check out our full review of the Tern GSD here .

Top speed: 32 km/h (20 mph) with electric assist
Range: 42-85 km (26-53 mi) depending on pedal input

Family Decides To Sell Their 1963 Pontiac, Driven One Day in Salt on Christmas Day in 1970
44 photos
Photo: eBay seller rimfire03581
Family-owned cars are the best cars, and this 1963 Pontiac Bonneville is nothing more than living proof. This specimen left the original owner after only one year - we all know many people gave up on their classics almost immediately after the purchase - and the Bonneville ended up under the roof of a family that retained it for decades.
That family is now ready to let it go, assuming someone with the right restoration skills comes across the listing and decides to take it home.
It’s pretty clear that this Bonneville is not supposed to be a daily driver. Not yet, at least, as the car needs some work, with the owner already completing several important repairs.
Photo: eBay seller rimfire03581 With the GTO not yet a thing in 1963, the Bonneville was often the Pontiac model that caught everybody’s attention in the early ‘60s. As the company's top full-size car, the Bonneville was supposed to impress in every single regard, including in terms of power.
The car was fitted with a 389ci engine that was equipped with a four-barrel carburetor and developed 235 horsepower. The same engine was also installed on other Pontiacs , but the Bonneville received an upgraded version that produced 20 horsepower more than on the rest of the cars.
The reason was simple: Pontiac wanted the Bonneville to be special, and increasing the power output allowed the car to catch everybody’s attention.
From a design perspective, the Bonneville didn’t receive significant tweaks until the 1964 model year when it got significantly closer to the coke bottle styling that we all know and love today. The 1963 model year witnessed the introduction of vertical headlights, with the Bonneville Custom wagon also getting the ax.
On the other hand, Pontiac still wanted wagons to be part of its offering, so despite the demise of the Custom wagon, it introduced the Bonneville Safari 4-door station wagon.
Photo: eBay seller rimfire03581 That is why the Bonneville can be easily considered a collectible, especially if it checks the right boxes. For example, original specimens that have never been restored or altered are more desirable than others, assuming they are already in good shape and don’t need major repairs.
The family that is currently caring for this Bonneville reveals that the car was driven in salt just one day, on Christmas day in 1970. Otherwise, it wasn’t necessarily abused, so the metal has passed the test of time with flying colors.
The original undercoating also helped. The Pontiac doesn’t suffer from major rust problems, but I would still inspect everything in person or, at least, order a third-party inspection to make sure the metal won’t require major repairs and the frame is still intact.
The car was repainted in the ‘70s to black, and the paint shows its age today. You can tell this is a project by just checking out the photos in the gallery, and I wonder where it’s been stored in the last couple of years, considering it’s now pictured outside.
Photo: eBay seller rimfire03581 As for the engine, we’re not getting many specifics, though it looks like the car is powered by a 389. The owner says they installed a new sending unit, a new carburetor and timing chain, but the car “still doesn’t run correctly.”
Theoretically, this isn’t necessarily a reason to walk away, as it means the engine is still alive, so a good mechanic is all it takes to bring the vehicle back to the road. Ask your mechanic to inspect this car live, and maybe with the right fixes, it would be much easier than initially thought to save it.
Otherwise, the car sells with many extra parts, so the restoration process - or, at least, what’s left from it - should be quite easy. The owner claims they don’t have the money or time to finish the project, so someone else must do it.
Photo: eBay seller rimfire03581 The selling price makes perfect sense, considering this is a project that will end up burning more dollars after it finds a new home. However, I do believe that any potential buyer would need additional information, and a walkaround video would certainly help, especially considering there are parts of the car that haven’t been exposed in the photos.
The owner believes that $6,500 is a fair price, and I don’t think they are far from the truth. This is a solid car where a significant part of the work has already been finished, so bringing it back to the road shouldn’t involve that much time and effort.
The bidding begins at $5,000, and considering this is a no-reserve auction, whoever sends the top offer can take it home in just a few days. The vehicle is parked in Lisbon, New Hampshire, and considering the engine doesn’t run correctly, you should also consider shipping cost to your garage. The listing is projected to go offline in just four days.

EICMA 2026 • Trio of New Morbidelli T802 Motorcycles Will Make Short Work of Every Surface
MTPeak Stole Some of the Spotlight at EICMA 2026 With Insane Power and Retro Looks on Three Wheels
37 photos
Photo: Cristian Curmei | Autoevolution
When you attend a motorcycle show, the last thing that you expect to steal the spotlight is a trike. Well, that’s precisely what MTPeak’s “roadster” has done, enticing countless EICMA 2026 visitors to stop by the booth and literally drool over what is in store for Europe and possibly the US in 2027.
EICMA IS the largest motorcycle show in the world, taking place in Milan year after year and spreading across several halls and over 3.5 million square feet. It also pulls in close to and sometimes exceeds 800,000 visitors from all over the world in just six days. It’s the literal place to be if you want to showcase motorcycles, ATVs, and other mobility solutions and witness them too.
Out of the hundreds to 1,000+ brands the show hosts every year, for the 83rd EICMA edition, one vehicle pulled me back to it time and time again over the course of the five days I was there.
Photo: Cristian Curmei | Autoevolution That vehicle is MTPeak’s “roadster,” for lack of a better word, or GTSport, and if looks alone didn’t get you to read this article, the specs for this thing will help you understand why I just couldn’t resist bringing it to light.
First and foremost, it’s clearly the design of this beast that caught the eye of countless passers-bys at EICMA. But that’s just the hook. As I dove deeper in the design with MTPeak’s own Anson Hu and Barry Ran, I just couldn’t believe what I was hearing.
Six hundred kilograms (1,322 lbs), carbon fiber panels, steel-cage design, three wheels, mid-mounted engine with turbo, detachable steering wheel, and a top speed of 180 kph (112 mph) which, mind you, you’ll reach relatively quickly.
But, before we go on, do take into consideration that what we witnessed at EICMA is a functioning proof of concept, and when and if mass production hits, some changes will clearly be made; MTPeak’s website mentions that a very limited production of just 100 units will take place.
Photo: Cristian Curmei | Autoevolution Now, what we’re looking at here is, as mentioned, a trike, set up with a single rear-mounted wheel and tire and two at the front, similar to a Can-Am Spyder and others on the market. Yet, you won’t be sitting in a saddle like you would on a Spyder, but rather, side by side with a passenger. It’s a very car-like interior, and not so moto.
On top of the three-wheel chassis, an automotive-grade steel cage is used to craft the base, along with a double wishbone suspension with twin dampers as standard. On top of that, Carbon fiber panels cover the frame in a retro and can’t-look-away design, forcing us to stare, if only for a few moments at a time.
That bodywork is all carbon fiber, and I can attest to that as I touched the underside of the paint job, but if you also get really close to it, you can faintly see the latticework of strands and fibers running under the paint. Since the underlying frame is one designed to be wider at the front and slimmer at the rear, an overall teardrop shape is brought to life.
Photo: Cristian Curmei | Autoevolution Yet, at ground level, when I first saw the two exhaust pipes running alongside the body, my first question was if this thing is electric and if they were only there for show. “No, it’s gas.” “Gas?! From a Chinese brand?” “Yes.” “Wow, sign me up!” That also when I remarked the gas tank mounted behind the driver and passenger’s headrests and realized its true use.
So, we have carbon fiber that results in a 600 kg vehicle, and one that looks very vintage as opposed to most of what EICMA offers, steel roll cage and chassis, and all built around a trike layout for heightened stability.
But, it’s what’s under the proverbial hood that matters most to you motorheads, and boy am I glad I chose to get closer to MTPeak’s team to see what makes this so special, aside from what I mentioned above.
At the heart of this showstopper is a 2-litre, mid-mounted engine that distributes the car’s weight perfectly down the middle and, if I may, cranks out a whipping 165 kW (221 hp) of power and a maximum of 385 Nm (284 lb-ft) of torque. Please take a moment to realize what that means for a vehicle that weighs 1,322 lbs.
Photo: Cristian Curmei | Autoevolution According to the folks at MTPeak, the GT is meant to be “a trike with car power,” and that’s a bit of an understatement; this thing is a gosh darned rocket! This grants the GT a top speed of as much as 180 kph (112 mph), and for something designed to rip up Europe’s rivieras, I’m so looking forward to taking this out for a spin. I’ll be working things out with MTPeak to do so in the coming months.
A lovely observation that a buddy of mine made was that this top speed is surely limited electronically, and that we should clearly be able to unlock more, depending on a few aspects, of course.
Currently, the GT is being exposed to the European market , with plans to actually bring it across to the US; interest from dealers already being shown, so if you cross your fingers, and wish really hard, you may just end up being a future owner of tester of a GT, and locally.
As for the experience of driving this one, clearly, we don’t have any idea of what that may be like just yet, but a 9-speed automatic transmission with reverse is part of the GT’s makeup, and so are the vented carbon-ceramic brakes for stopping power and control. There’s also a mention in the spec sheet that power to weight ratio stands at 370 hp per tonne (1.1 US ton).
Photo: Cristian Curmei | Autoevolution A few other traits that you need to be aware of in case this ride stole your heart too, include the steering wheel, which is removable – the GT won’t start without it – and an interior that, currently, is still in the works, hence the simple and rather drab vinyl flooring and faux leather seats and armrests that are literally part of the body. If enough interest is gauged here, we’re sure to be able to expect a different interior.
Currently, pricing has not yet been revealed and according to the folks at MTPeak, the GT will also have an electric variant in the works; simply put, people are asking for it.
The question is: Who the heck is MTPeak and where did they come from? Well, believe it or not, MTPeak is an off-shoot brand of Chongqing Guangyu Motorcycle, a China-born team that has been in the motorcycle and vehicle market since 1996. That's 30 years of experience pumped into the GT.
Photo: Cristian Curmei | Autoevolution While the GT isn’t hammer-and-chiseled into stone just yet, the plans are to have it in the market in 2027. I can’t wait!
I’m curious to hear your thoughts on this EICMA gem and what it brings to the table; there’s a comment section below where you can leave your thoughts.
